status: drafted via direct read of the real Ethiopian-translation extracted verse text (Assets/Resources/Verses/Ethiopian/song_of_solomon_32.json), cross-checked against the existing KJV Character Index entry for tier-naming-style reference only
notes: Read the full 8-chapter, 117-verse Ethiopian-translation text directly before drafting. Verse-by-verse comparison against the KJV Song of Solomon found NO real content or structural differences for this book in this source: identical chapter count (8), identical verse count per chapter (17,17,11,16,16,13,13,14 = 117), and identical wording throughout (e.g. 1:1 'The song of songs, which is Solomon's'; 6:13's lone 'Shulamite' naming; 8:6-7's 'love is strong as death' passage) - this is a genuine case where the Ethiopian source's Song of Solomon text matches the standard canon exactly, unlike some other books in this project (e.g. this translation's own distinct 'Ezra'). Because of that, this book's structure necessarily mirrors the KJV index's own reasoning: it is dialogue/poetry, not narrative, with only two speaking voices throughout (Solomon and the Shulamite) plus one famous named theme-passage (Love As Strong As Death, 8:6-7) and three minor supporting collectives (the daughters of Jerusalem, the city watchmen, and the Shulamite's unnamed brothers) attached as submanagers under her tier. All character/manager ids are suffixed _eth_sos to avoid any collision with the existing KJV CharacterIndex ids (solomon, shulamite, love_strong_as_death, etc.) or with any future translation's ids for this same book. No naming collisions were found within the book itself - only two named/titled figures appear (Solomon by name, the Shulamite by gentilic), with every other party (daughters of Jerusalem, watchmen, brothers, Solomon's 'threescore queens and fourscore concubines') left as an anonymous collective exactly as the text itself leaves them - none are individually differentiated by the text, so none are invented as individuals.

characters.name: Solomon

genealogy.note: Father/mother per the wider biblical record, not restated within this book itself. The text distinguishes the Shulamite from his 'threescore queens, and fourscore concubines, and virgins without number' (6:8-9) as the one he calls uniquely 'my dove, my undefiled... the only one.'

verses.note: Opening line attributes the whole poem to him: 'The song of songs, which is Solomon's.'
Praises her, comparing her to 'a company of horses in Pharaoh's chariots,' promising 'borders of gold with studs of silver.'
Calls her fair, 'thou hast doves' eyes.'
Answers her rose-of-Sharon self-description: 'As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters.'
His invitation speech recalled in his own words: 'Rise up, my love, my fair one, and come away,' describing spring's arrival.
Calls her 'my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock,' asking to see her face and hear her voice.

His wedding-day procession: 'King Solomon made himself a chariot of the wood of Lebanon' with silver pillars and a purple covering, escorted by 'threescore valiant men'; his mother's crown 'in the day of his espousals.'
First head-to-foot praise (hair, teeth, lips, temples, neck, breasts), closing 'thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee.'
Addresses her as 'my sister, my spouse,' likening her to 'a garden inclosed... a fountain sealed' filled with spice trees.
Answers he has 'come into my garden, my sister, my spouse,' inviting friends to 'eat... drink abundantly.'

Second head-to-foot/city praise: 'fair as Tirzah, comely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army with banners' (6:4), repeated at the close (6:10); sets her apart from the 'threescore queens... fourscore concubines' as 'the only one' (6:8-9).
'I went down into the garden of nuts' - traditionally read as his voice.
Third head-to-foot praise, feet to head this time: 'How fair and how pleasant art thou, O love, for delights!'
Asks to hear her voice once more: 'the companions hearken to thy voice: cause me to hear it.'

funFacts: The book's opening line attributes it to him directly: 'The song of songs, which is Solomon's' (1:1).
Praises the Shulamite in three separate head-to-foot passages across the book (4:1-7; 6:4-10; 7:1-9), each with different imagery.
His wedding-day palanquin of Lebanon cedar with silver pillars and a purple covering gets more physical description than any other object in the book (3:6-11).
6:8-9 names 'threescore queens, and fourscore concubines, and virgins without number,' but sets the Shulamite apart from all of them as 'the only one.'

characters.name: The Shulamite

genealogy.note: Called only 'the Shulamite' (6:13) - a gentilic, not a personal name, used exactly once in the book. Her mother is mentioned but never named (1:6; 8:1-2; 8:5); her father is never mentioned at all. Addressed as Solomon's 'spouse' from 4:8 onward and as sharing in his 'espousals' (3:11).

verses.note: Opens the book with her own longing: 'Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth... Draw me, we will run after thee.'
'I am black, but comely'; explains it as sun-darkening from being made 'the keeper of the vineyards' by her mother's angry children.
Asks where he pastures his flock at noon; answered to follow 'the footsteps of the flock' if she does not know.
While the king sits at his table, she is 'a bundle of myrrh' and 'a cluster of camphire' to him.
Returns his praise: 'Behold, thou art fair, my beloved... also our bed is green.'
Names herself: 'I am the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valleys.'
Likens him to 'the apple tree among the trees of the wood'; first of the book's three-times-repeated charge to the daughters of Jerusalem not to 'stir up... love, till he please.'
'Take us the foxes, the little foxes, that spoil the vines'; closes 'My beloved is mine, and I am his.'
First search begins: seeks him 'by night on my bed,' finds him not, rises to 'go about the city' seeking him.
The city watchmen find her; she asks, 'Saw ye him whom my soul loveth?'
Just past the watchmen she finds him: 'I held him, and would not let him go,' bringing him to 'my mother's house.'
Second occurrence of the charge to the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love before its time.
Invites the winds to her garden so its spices flow out, and calls her beloved into it.
Second search begins: 'I sleep, but my heart waketh,' hears him knock, delays too long, opens to find 'my beloved had withdrawn himself.'
This time the watchmen 'smote me... wounded me,' taking her veil.
Third occurrence of the charge to the daughters of Jerusalem.
The daughters ask what sets her beloved apart from any other.
Her own head-to-foot praise of him in reply, closing 'he is altogether lovely... this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.'
The daughters ask where he has gone; she answers he is 'gone down into his garden,' closing 'I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine.'
Named here only: 'Return, return, O Shulamite.'
'I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me'; invites him to the vineyards and villages.
Wishes he 'wert as my brother'; fourth and final charge to the daughters of Jerusalem.
Asked, 'Who is this that cometh up from the wilderness, leaning upon her beloved?'; recalled being raised up and born 'under the apple tree.'
'Set me as a seal upon thine heart... love is strong as death... many waters cannot quench love.'
Her brothers debate how to guard 'our sister' when the time comes that 'she shall be spoken for.'
Answers them: 'I am a wall, and my breasts like towers: then was I in his eyes as one that found favour.'
Contrasts Solomon's leased-out vineyard at Baal-hamon with her own, kept for herself: 'my vineyard, which is mine, is before me.'
The book's final line, her closing words to him: 'Make haste, my beloved... upon the mountains of spices.'

funFacts: Speaks more of the book's lines than any other voice, and frames both of its search-and-reunion sequences (3:1-5; 5:2-6:3).
Describes herself as 'black, but comely' from sun exposure while forced to keep her brothers' vineyards (1:5-6), then closes the book still speaking in vineyard imagery of her own (8:12).
Delivers the book's most quoted lines on the nature of love - 'love is strong as death... many waters cannot quench love' (8:6-7).
The watchmen who simply encounter her on her first search (3:3) turn violent on her second, striking her and taking her veil (5:7).

characters.name: Love As Strong As Death
characters.purpose: Declares the nature of love itself - as strong as death, its jealousy unyielding as the grave, burning like the fiercest flame, unquenchable by any flood, and beyond purchase at any price.

verses.note: 'Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame.'
'Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it'; love cannot be bought 'for the substance of his house.'

funFacts: Spoken by the Shulamite directly to Solomon, not by a narrator or a third party.
One of the most-quoted passages in the entire Bible on the nature of love.
Uses fire/flame imagery ('coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame') found nowhere else in the book's otherwise garden-and-spice vocabulary.

characters.name: Daughters of Jerusalem
characters.perkNote: The bride's circle of companions and witnesses - repeatedly charged by her not to awaken love before its time (2:7; 3:5; 8:4), and the ones she turns to for reassurance in 5:9 and 6:1.

genealogy.note: An anonymous chorus of young women, companions to the Shulamite; no individual genealogy is given for any of them, matching how the text itself leaves them undifferentiated.

verses.note: First charge: 'that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.'
Second identical charge, repeated word for word.
Charged a third time, then ask her what makes her beloved better than any other.
Ask where her beloved has gone so they can seek him with her.
Fourth and final repetition of the charge.

funFacts: Addressed with the same near-identical refrain, 'I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem... that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please,' at 2:7, 3:5, and 8:4.
The only ones in the book who ask the Shulamite a direct question about her beloved (5:9).

characters.name: The Watchmen
characters.perkNote: Patrol the city she searches by night - a neutral presence on her first search (3:3), but strike her and take her veil on the second (5:7).

genealogy.note: Anonymous city guards; no genealogy is given for them in the text.

verses.note: Encountered on her first search; she asks if they have seen her beloved.
On her second search they turn violent: 'they smote me, they wounded me... took away my veil.'

funFacts: Their role shifts sharply between the book's two search sequences: helpful bystanders in 3:3, violent in 5:7.

characters.name: The Shulamite's Brothers
characters.perkNote: Set her to labor keeping the family vineyards as a girl (1:6), then debate how to guard her honor as a woman in 8:8-9 - answered by her own declaration, 'I am a wall' (8:10).

genealogy.note: Referred to only as 'my mother's children' (1:6), never individually named; their father is never mentioned.

verses.note: Called 'my mother's children'; angry with her, they made her 'keeper of the vineyards.'
Discuss what to do for their 'little sister... in the day when she shall be spoken for.'

funFacts: Their plan for their 'little sister' in 8:8-9 is directly answered by her own words in the very next verse, 8:10.

genealogyLists.note: No bulk/unresolved genealogical references needed for this book - it names only two figures directly (Solomon, the Shulamite) and leaves every other party as an anonymous collective (daughters of Jerusalem, watchmen, brothers, queens/concubines) exactly as the text itself does, so nothing further to log here.
